  infinitesimal and tangent spaces using the concept of inverse limits, which
  enabled us to define differentiable structures on these spaces. We then proved
  the existence of a mapping between the tangent space and the space of all
  infinitesimal combinations of expressions. Finally, we formulated an
  infinitesimal version of the Schröder-Einstein notation and showed that it can
  be used to describe combinations of expressions, which generalizes the
  combinatory logic concept of combining terms with combinators. Notably, our
  approach provides a new understanding of the expression $(\;,\;)$ as a
  differential operator that maps pairs of expressions to combinations of those
  expressions. We also explored the application of our work on the combinatory
  logic expressions to the concept of a C-space, which is a fundamental aspect of
  the differential logic framework. Ultimately, our study provides a unified
  mathematical foundation for the differential and combinatory approaches to
  logic, as well as an introduction to the concepts of infinitesimal and
  tangent spaces. These innovations open the door to examining traditional
  combinatory logic in a new light and may also facilitate the extension of

  Advances in computer tomography and image analysis enable doctors to accurately 
  diagnose lung diseases by examining CT scans, yet existing systems are often too

  accessible system for monitoring lung health by leveraging advances in AI and 
  applying it to data from portable breathing sensors. To achieve this, a large 
  dataset of breathing signals was collected from participants wearing CT scanners 
  and respiratory sensors, in collaboration with the University of Manchester and 
  Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust. This dataset, known as the MRC-Lung 
  dataset, consists of 1,440 breathing cycles from 30 subjects with varying lung 
  diseases. Initial experiments using this dataset revealed promising results for 
  classifying lung conditions using shallow machine learning models. Future studies 
  will build on these findings by expanding the dataset to enable the development 
  of more sophisticated AI systems for at-home lung health monitoring. 
  Preliminary data collected from 30 participants shows that distinct breathing 
  patterns can be accurately detected using machine learning models. Notably, this 
  study demonstrates that AI-powered systems can effectively classify patients with 
  various lung conditions, including COPD, pneumonia, lung cancer, and heart disease, 
  using data from non-invasive respiratory sensors. With an expanded dataset, it's 
  possible that such systems could empower individuals to track their lung health 
  remotely and schedule medical consultations only when necessary. 
  Although AI-powered systems for at-home monitoring hold great promise, the 
  research community still needs to collect more data to develop a more extensive 
  and reliable dataset for training. This study serves as a starting point, and 
  future work will focus on enhancing the MRC-Lung dataset to enable the creation 
  of more advanced AI models for accurately classifying various lung conditions. 
  Initial findings using shallow machine learning models on the current dataset 
  indicate that distinct breathing patterns can accurately be detected. With a 
  larger, more diverse dataset, researchers can develop AI models that utilize more 
  complex machine learning algorithms, leading to more precise lung disease 
  classification. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the 
  development of reliable, user-friendly AI systems for at-home lung health 
  monitoring, empowering individuals to track their lung health remotely and seek 
  medical attention when necessary.

A key aspect in designing a practical radar system is reducing communication overhead, which can be achieved by compactly storing and efficiently transmitting the data sent from the sensor to the processor. Given the current complexity of JPDA solutions, there is a need for a more efficient approach to streamline this process. This paper introduces a novel solution that transforms the standard JPDA algorithm to tackle the challenges of data storage and efficient communication, resulting in two primary formulations. The first formulation yields a detailed probability distribution, while the second generates a compact probabilistic summary. Both formulations are resolved through a matrix multiplication approach, which is then tested on realistic data and shown to outperform existing solutions in terms of efficiency. The proof of convergence for the second formulation is also provided, demonstrating that significant reductions in communication overhead can be achieved. Specifically, this approach enables storing and transmitting data within a small dimensionality of $O(K^2)$, where $K$ represents the number of targets, rather than the traditional $O(KKM)$ with $M$ being the number of measurements per target. This breakthrough offers substantial improvements in data storage and communication efficiency, especially in large-scale multiple-target scenarios. The proposed approach is expected to revolutionize the design of practical radar systems, enabling seamless data transmission and efficient processing. In this study, we explore the potential of collaborative multi-agent art as a reflection of human creativity. We also investigate whether it can serve as a reliable indicator of its underlying generative model. To this end, we introduce a new assessment method for generative models, which we refer to as the Artistic Homogeneity Index. This method evaluates the diversity of artistic outputs produced by multiple agents, each generated from a single, training model. We put this new index to use in examining the impact of different model types on artistic homogeneity. Additionally, we use color palettes from famous human art movements to illustrate how the choice of model output distribution affects the visual cohesion of artistic creations. Ultimately, our study demonstrates the utility of the Artistic Homogeneity Index as a tool for analyzing the properties of generative models used in creating collaborative multi-agent art. It also sheds light on the artistic movements that share similar characteristics with the outputs produced by these models. On a broader scale, our research may serve as a starting point for a more in-depth connection between the study of human art and the development of AI-generated collaborative multi-agent art. Data analysis has become increasingly sophisticated, incorporating complex models of the systems involved. However, the existing Gaussian Process method used to mitigate stationary noise in the data, when combined with the growing number of signals detected, has led to significant computational difficulties in the parameter estimation process. As a result, there is a pressing need for improved methods to analyze the data accurately within a reasonable timeframe. In an effort to address this challenge, we propose an optimized method based on the Lefebvre algorithm, which outperforms traditional approaches by reducing the computational burden while maintaining high levels of accuracy in the data fits. In addition, we have developed a novel method for determining the optimal regularization parameters in the data fits, which is both efficient and reliable. Our analysis indicates that this new method aligns well with conventional methods, but is particularly effective for short data sets, reducing the computational time by a factor of three to four without compromising the levels of accuracy achieved. In light of these breakthroughs, we are confident that our methods will play a vital role in the analysis of the next generation of gravitational wave data, which is poised to be dominated by numerous signals from merging neutron star compact binaries. Ultimately, our work is expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of these celestial events and the characteristics of neutron stars. Although there are established connections between these matrix elements and electromagnetic processes, detailed relationships remain scarce, particularly for processes involving nucleons and isospin-violating reactions. However, we've found a new method to quickly lower an particle's velocity using less light, which makes the process more efficient. In this study, we address a more practical issue by exploring how to efficiently implement a basic yet effective algorithm - Personalized Graph Walk - on general-purpose GPU architectures. Graph Walk involves randomly walking through graphs to generate candidates for unsatisfied user needs. Our implementation, however, encounters significant memory and processing limitations. The treatment regimen is composed of two medications: one that inhibits the growth of the tumor and another that slows down the formation of new blood vessels. We analyze different boundary and initial conditions in the optimisation problem to represent scenarios where the tumor is contained by a physical barrier and scenarios where it is not. We use analytical methods to solve this problem in simple cases, and numerical techniques such as the finite element method to solve more complex cases. The results show that the most effective treatment typically targets both the tumor and the blood vessel growth. We found that in some situations, inhibiting the blood vessel growth is more crucial than inhibiting the tumor growth, and that applying medication uniformly throughout the tumor is not always the most effective approach. However, the number of unknown protein structures far exceeds the number that can be studied using current X-ray crystallography methods. To address this issue, the Rosetta ab initio protein structure prediction method was developed to accurately predict protein structures based solely on protein sequence information. In the Rosetta ab initio approach, the search for the optimal protein structure involves the assembly of protein fragments and the refinement of their spatial arrangements. In a 2018 Community-Wide experiment, the Rosetta ab initio method was tested against other prediction methods using a large dataset of protein sequences. To improve the accuracy of the Rosetta ab initio method, the incorporation of additional data, such as protein structures observed under different conditions and predicted protein structures based on similarity to other proteins, has enhanced the method's performance. In a 2021 Community-Wide experiment, the updated Rosetta ab initio method was tested and demonstrated improved predictions compared to other methods. The results from these experiments have laid the groundwork for the development of next-generation protein structure prediction methods that incorporate a wide range of protein-related data. Furthermore, the potential for the integration of the Rosetta ab initio method with other protein structure prediction methods that predict the arrangement of protein sequences into 3D structures is explored. Our research focuses on the properties of the acoustic phonons in arrays of nanotubes using complex optical simulations. The findings show that arranging nanotubes in a square lattice naturally produces modes with specific k-vector characteristics. Additionally, it was discovered that varying the diameter of each nanotube significantly influences the gap magnitude and shape, especially for larger diameters where the gap narrows. Unlike spherical particles, nanotubes allow for the existence of multiple plasmon-phonon coupling events within a specific region. The underlying cause of these interactions can be attributed to the unique relationship between the curvature of the light field and the geometric characteristics of the nanotubes. This effect is particularly pronounced for 2nd order plasmon-phonon coupling and tends to strengthen as the tubes undergo cylindrical deformation. Our research highlights the potential for acoustic phonons in arrays of cylinders to significantly expand the range of plasmon-phonon coupling, which could lead to innovative applications in plasmon-assisted phonon engineering. Our work also provides a theoretical foundation for the investigation of plasmon-phonon coupling in arrays of nanotubes and nanowires. Research has shown that artificial neural networks often require significantly more parameters and connections than the human brain to achieve comparable performance, a problem known as the "missing synapse problem." Moreover, even state-of-the-art neural networks lack a clear correspondence with brain regions, a problem known as the "missing region problem." These challenges highlight the immense difficulty of reverse-engineering the human brain, a problem that may be insurmountable with our current understanding of the brain and artificial neural networks.

lecture notes from a 2020 course taught by Alejandro Arvin at the Universidad Autonoma de Mexico. The course covered the basics of ergodic theory and measure theory, focusing on finite measure spaces. The notes begin by reviewing basic topological concepts before diving into sigma-algebras, measurable functions, and the construction of measure spaces. After establishing the necessary tools, the course delves into the core topics of ergodic theory, including Caratheodory measures, the Caratheodory algebras, Borel sets, the continuum hypothesis, Radon measures, the Stone-Weierstrass theorem, and separable metric spaces. Additionally, the course included an exploration of Banach spaces, linear operators, and the basic principles of integration theory, before specifically analyzing measure-algebra homomorphisms and the unique representation of measures on specific algebras in relation to certain properties of projections in $L^\infty$ spaces. The course culminated by investigating basic ergodic theory concepts for measure-preserving transformations, including Borel probability spaces, the construction of shift-invariant sigma-algebras, the ergodicity of translations on compact spaces, the ergodic hulls of transformations, the counting measure on countable discrete spaces, and the analysis of continuous maps on compact intervals of the real line. The lecture notes also include relevant results from general topology and the properties of complete metric spaces.  The content of the course was adapted from the 1969-1970 lectures by R. Ellis, the 1975-1976 lectures by D.A. Burkholder, and the 1981-1982 lectures by R. Kaufman, with additional insights from various other sources.  The course was taught to a group of graduate students at the Universidad Autonoma de Mexico, and the material was presented in Spanish. In an effort to address these issues and develop a more versatile and adaptable system for semantic unit extraction within patent texts, this research proposes a novel, rule-based approach. Furthermore, our approach exhibits greater robustness in the face of noisy data, maintaining its performance even when confronted with flawed CMT documents, whereas the base model's performance significantly declines in such scenarios. Meeting the demanding requirements of 5G and future networks in terms of reliability, data rate, and packet transmission latency is challenging with traditional single-channel transmission methods. This problem can be addressed by employing multi-carrier transmission techniques like OFDMA, which allocate resources independently to mobile devices and network managers. However, using multi-carrier transmission comes with performance limitations due to narrow bandwidth allocation and rapid changes in wireless propagation channels. To overcome these limitations, this research introduces a hybrid approach combining block-wise multi-carrier transmission with a technique adapted from deep learning methods to create a dynamic framing algorithm. The proposed algorithm, DBMF, can provide a balance between the amount of resources allocated and the quality of those resources, leading to improved performance in dynamic environments. The framework's efficiency was verified through a comparison of our approach with existing optimized algorithms, demonstrating its potential to achieve better results. Specifically, DBMF outperformed existing solutions by enhancing the average effective throughput by 47.2% and the packet delivery ratio by 44.9%, with an increased average transmission latency of 13.2%. The framework's effectiveness was further validated through real-time implementation using a Zynq-7000 FPGA board, yielding a substantial reduction of 35.1% in computational complexity. Overall, the DBMF approach offers a dynamic, efficient, and practical solution for resource allocation in 5G wireless networks. The framework's potential to adapt to a variety of applications also makes it an attractive option for future network design. This study focuses on whether people agree or disagree with others in news comments, particularly regarding the COVID-19 pandemic, by examining opinions on vaccination mandates. We analyzed a large dataset of 181 online news articles from five significant German newspapers, collected over a year following the pandemic's onset. initial investigation, we studied how a small piece of tape attached to the surface of a viscous fluid affects its flow. Specifically, we considered a situation where the tape is long compared to the distance over which the fluid's properties vary. Our research focused on how the tape's presence influences mass transport in the fluid near its surface. We found that its impact is determined by the balance between the tape's length and the distance the fluid molecules can travel before their memory of the initial conditions fades. If the tape is long enough, its attachment creates a region around it where the fluid's flow is actually slowed down, even when considering the overall movement of the fluid. This effect is notable in thin layers of fluid and plays a significant role in mass transport. Our findings are relevant to various situations in which small objects influence heat or mass transfer within a fluid. As a result, there is a pressing need for intelligent resource allocation mechanisms that effectively handle and learn the properties of various types of network data.  Inspired by human behavior, cognitive learning can be applied to develop and adapt such mechanisms.  In this paper, we introduce CLORA, a novel, cognitive approach to resource allocation in wireless networks that utilizes a dual-mode learning mechanism to optimize resource sharing. This technique, which has been employed by computers for just as long, involves generating or creating programs based on given requirements. There are several program synthesis methods, with some computers producing programs by trial and error and others by first developing a detailed plan for the program before writing it. This study focuses on a form of program synthesis known as inverse synthesis, which involves defining a high-level description of a desired program and then using computer algorithms to produce a detailed, executable version. One of the key challenges in inverse synthesis is accurately translating the program description into a detailed specification, a task made even more difficult when considering abstract program descriptions. This study presents a novel inverse synthesis approach, called Abstract Inverse Synthesis, that uses examples to define a program's behavior and maps abstract program descriptions to detailed specifications using a graph representation. This approach is demonstrated through the development of a system called AbSynth, which successfully inverts specifications of multiple string sorting algorithms across various character sets after being trained on a dataset consisting of a single example for each specification. This study further examines the capabilities and limitations of AbSynth through multiple evaluation processes and highlights potential future research areas for the approach. The source code for AbSynth and its data sets can be found at: https://github.com/ramramlt/AbSynth. The experiments were supported by the computing resources at the University of Colorado Boulder. Firstly, we will demonstrate the process of backprojection using convolution kernels, thereby illustrating the equivalence of the forward operator in computed tomography (CT) and the adjoint of the convolution operator. This realization leads to a formulation of CT reconstruction as a deconvolution problem. Secondly, we will show how this deconvolution approach can be extended to handle analytic imaging techniques, specifically by incorporating the effects of nearest neighbor, bilinear, and boxwise extrapolation operators. The results show that the use of the exact kernel outperforms its approximated counterparts in the CT reconstruction process. However, for scenarios where only approximated kernels are available, our method still yields satisfactory CT reconstructions. This contributes a new perspective to the field of CT reconstruction and offers an innovative solution for such situations where only approximated kernels can be employed. Initially, we examine a distributed graph in which every node initiates a process and every edge has a unique label. Our aim is to identify the minimum number of messages required for these tasks. Interestingly, we find that both voting and sorting operations necessitate at least O(n log n) messages. To confirm the necessity of this bound, we present a specific algorithm that accomplishes these tasks using exactly O(n log n) messages. Our findings yield an interesting conclusion - the message complexity of these tasks is directly dependent on the graph's depth, which is essentially the number of edges within the graph. This discovery also gives rise to a new question: what is the minimum message complexity when dealing with a complete graph in a distributed setting? To investigate this, we develop a new algorithm for both voting and sorting operations that achieve a message complexity of O(n polylog n), indicating a significant improvement in scalability. Lastly, we explore the feasibility of further reductions in message complexity by investigating a simplified graph structure known as a tree. Through our analysis, we establish tight bounds for the message complexity of voting and sorting operations in a distributed tree, ultimately revealing an interesting duality between these tasks. Specifically, we find that while sorting may necessitate more messages than voting in general graphs, the opposite holds true in a distributed tree setting. Our research on sorting in trees also highlights an interesting connection to a well-known counting problem in a central collector model. Our work ultimately demonstrates that both voting and sorting operations can be performed efficiently within a distributed tree, achieving a message complexity of O(log^2 n). This discovery is significant as it represents one of the most efficient known solutions to these tasks. To confirm the necessity of this bound, we present a new lower bound proof, showcasing the difficulty of performing these tasks in a distributed setting. This research contributes to a broader understanding of the trade-offs between communication efficiency and the complexity of the graph structure in a distributed setting. Finally, we investigate the feasibility of one-round solutions for voting and sorting operations in a distributed setting. Through our analysis, we find that while sorting may be performed efficiently in a single round, the same may not be said for voting. To address this discrepancy, we develop a novel approach, involving a specific graph structure known as a binary tree with fake nodes, that allows us to create a one-round solution for sorting. Our work ultimately leads to a new lower bound proof for the message complexity of voting and sorting operations

a single infected individual within a subset of interconnected households is a crucial factor in pandemic modeling and is influenced by various factors such as household size, the probability of being infected within a household, and contact patterns specific to households.  A common approach in the epidemiological literature involves averaging the expected number of secondary infections over different possible household sizes, however this method can lead to inaccuracies.  In the current study, we have derived formulas for the variance and standard deviation of the number of secondary infections, given certain assumptions regarding mixing patterns in households.  The results show that averaging the expected number of secondary infections by household size actually equals half of the variance divided by the expected value, implying that estimating this value using the average of the expected number of secondary infections underdispersed, or has less variability than the actual count.  The results were validated through simulations using data from US and UK surveillance projects.  The findings of this study provide a framework for improving the accuracy of pandemic modeling by utilizing the actual distribution of outcomes, rather than approximating them with the average of the expected values.  The method can be applied to various other scenarios beyond pandemic modeling, where outcomes are averaged over different possible group sizes.  In such cases, utilizing the actual distribution of outcomes, rather than approximating them with the average of the expected values, can lead to more precise estimates. This paper presents an alternative variant, using a firework-like representation of edges, and provides a clear definition of emptiness. Furthermore, by demonstrating the inclusion of this model into the L$\forall$2 logic, we show that checking emptiness is computationally complex, specifically PSPACE-complete. This complexity holds true even in restricted scenarios, such as when event durations are constant or when the number of past events is limited. However, when all event durations are fixed at 0, the model can be equivalently represented using just ordinary automata, and the associated emptiness problem becomes simply P-complete. This highlights a significant jump in complexity when considering the dynamic nature of event clocks with variable durations. To further validate the model, we successfully apply it to two real-world verification tasks. First, we show its ability to effectively monitor safety properties in a model of growing memory, which traditional approaches cannot. Second, we use the model to recast and demonstrate the correctness of a well-known mathematical proof for proving language inclusion between two different types of automata. Overall, the firework model offers a more intuitive and expressive means of dynamic system monitoring. Its results can be seen as a form of'syntactic type checking' for ensuring that a system's behavior remains within specified constraints over time. The model's associated tools and techniques offer promising avenues for future research in dynamic system monitoring. These capabilities can be utilized through the online Firewafer tool, which allows users to define and verify properties for dynamic systems described as timed pushdown stacks. This model has already shown its utility in verifying a variety of significant applications. One notable example involves proving that a particular algorithm remains within memory limits when processing recursive structures. Another significant area involves verifying the correctness of compiled code translated from C programs, which involves proving that memory allocation and deallocation remain synchronized. The model has also been used to verify safety properties in complex domains, such as air traffic control systems. These applications, along with many more, demonstrate the model's practical value and its potential for a wide range of future research and development. This research investigates a specific WSM system and observes a transition from a quantum Hall state to a non-Hermitian topological phase. When a magnetic field is applied, the WSM system undergoes a gapped transformation due to spin-orbit coupling. By adjusting an anti-spin-orbit coupling parameter, the system's self-averaged localization properties emerge around the Dirac points. Both one-dimensional edge states and two-dimensional bulk states exhibit the predicted behavior. Notably, in the presence of a finite magnetic field, the bulk states transition from extended states to self-localized states, characterized by a specific Y-shaped wave function. Conversely, in the absence of a magnetic field, the system remains Hermitian and exhibits no localization. This study provides crucial insights into the behavior of WSM systems under magnetic fields and potential pathways to realize exotic quantum phases. Moreover, the resulting localized states display unique characteristics that could be valuable for quantum information applications. Finally, the research explores the potential connections to recent experiments on WSM systems. This study's findings are expected to contribute to the growing field of non-Hermitian topological electronics. Yet, the conventional representation of SDN, built upon graph theory, has inherent limitations in capturing dynamic network data. This leads to a range of issues including the complexity of programming, reduced visibility of network information, and degraded ability to handle network problems. To address these challenges, a relational SDN model has been proposed, leveraging first-order logic to provide clear and concise semantic rules for data manipulation. This model incorporates attributes from graph theory but also enables accurate and precise querying of network data, thus improving programming clarity and network problem resolution. Furthermore, relational SDN exhibits better scalability and is more adaptable to diverse data sources compared to its graph-based counterpart. To validate its effectiveness, an open-source platform for OpenFlow networks was developed, based on the relational SDN model, and thorough experiments were conducted to demonstrate its advantages in programming simplicity, data querying capabilities, and scalability. Specifically, the results show that with the same level of network traffic, the relational SDN model can achieve up to 3 times faster flow table management compared to the traditional approach. Additionally, when network traffic increases, the model exhibits linear scalability in data querying and network optimization operations, whereas the traditional approach experiences exponential growth in both areas. These findings firmly establish the relational SDN model as a superior alternative for programming and network operations. Ultimately, the successful implementation of this model can contribute to advancements in multiple fields, including artificial intelligence for network management, through the open-source platform used in the experiments. This work also paves the way for exploring applications of the relational SDN model in emerging technologies like software-defined storage, as well as providing insights into the design of more efficient programming languages for SDN. Finally, the relational SDN model has potential implications for the development of formal specification methods for data processing and network management, potentially extending to verified compiler design. Within the cores of white dwarfs, specifically near their centers, ULA potentials can cause variations in electron number density, thereby inducing an electric dipole that generates a magnetic field.  This research calculates the magnetic field produced by such an effect within the cores of white dwarfs, using numerical solutions to the Laplace equation and averaging methods.  The results indicate that, for a particular range of ULA masses and at the centers of white dwarfs, the induced electric dipole's magnetic field can be substantial, potentially affecting electron spin alignment in these stars.  The magnitude of the magnetic field produced by this electrostatic effect is comparable to, or even greater than, the dynamo-generated magnetic field observed in some white dwarf cores.  The research also identifies limitations and possible applications of the phenomenon in supernova explosions and core-collapse supernovae.  Ultimately, further investigation into the phenomenon is necessary to fully understand its implications for the observed properties of white dwarf cores. This formalism is verified in scenarios with both attractive and repulsive interactions and comparisons are made with existing results from the literature. Additionally, the momentum distribution is investigated for a gas of bosons in a toroidal trap, yielding new analytical expressions that are consistent with numerical data obtained via the Bogoliubov approximation. This work explores the momentum distribution in scenarios where the virial expansion converges slowly or irregularly. The findings suggest the existence of distinct regimes in the momentum distribution, characterized by the relative strengths of the radial force applied by the trap and the mean-field interaction, as well as the degeneracy parameter. The momentum distribution in a toroidal trap is found to depend on the relative strengths of these forces and the quantum degeneracy parameter $\gamma$. In this context, the momentum distribution is shown to exhibit a non-monotonous dependence on $\gamma$ when the radial force is weaker than the interaction, displaying a maximum at an intermediate $\gamma$ value. Conversely, in scenarios where the radial force exceeds the interaction, the momentum distribution monotonously increases with $\gamma$. source of information - speech prosody.  This feature plays a key role in how we convey meaning and emotion in speech.  Unfortunately, current models used for speech recognition often neglect prosody or require specialized annotation, a time-consuming and costly process.  Instead, we've developed a novel framework that leverages the relationships between audio signals and prosodic features within speech data.  This model extracts prosody from speech signals without the need for manual annotation, producing more accurate results than models that rely on limited, carefully annotated data.  When combined with existing speech recognition models, our approach leads to significant improvements in word and phoneme accuracy across multiple languages.  For example, in English, our model reduces the word error rate by 8.3% and phoneme error rate by 8.3%, achieving similar gains in Dutch, Japanese, and Korean.  Furthermore, our model effectively captures long-term audio patterns, allowing it to achieve impressive results even when as much as 20 milliseconds of the surrounding context is removed.  At the heart of our model lies a novel attention mechanism, called self-attention over frames (SAF), that enables it to analyze the audio signal on a frame-by-frame basis.  By using the output from a pre-trained deep neural network as input, the SAF model is able to identify the most relevant audio segments to focus on, effectively determining which parts of the speech signal contain the most useful information.  Through extensive testing, we've demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach in a range of scenarios, including the recognition of out-of-vocabulary words, identification of spoken dialogue acts, and the integration with other deep learning models to improve their accuracy.  Ultimately, our framework has the potential to unlock a wide range of innovative applications for speech prosody.  Through the open-source release of our code and data, we aim to facilitate further research and development in this exciting field.  Additional resources, including the model and data, can be found at https://github.com/keunwoo/librosa-prosody. military equipment in aerial images is a critical problem with significant implications for security and surveillance. The task is complex due to variables like lighting, terrain, and the size and orientation of objects. The emergence of large-scale datasets and advanced deep learning methods, particularly for image classification and object detection, has significantly impacted the field, but a major obstacle remains: the scarcity of high-quality datasets specifically for anomaly detection. To fill this gap, we created a large collection of 287k images showing various types of equipment, taken from Google Earth, and utilized it to develop a benchmark dataset with a built-in evaluation mechanism. Our proposed approach leverages pre-trained models, specifically a SwAV encoder and a DeiT classifier, to enhance performance, and our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this method, with the simplified method also showing promise on a separate military equipment dataset. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/alexeygrig/AnomalyDetectionAerialImages. 

  This research paper introduces a novel approach for detecting anomalies in aerial images using a combination of pre-trained models. Specifically, it leverages a SwAV encoder, which is trained on the massive ImageNet-22K dataset, and pairs it with a DeiT classifier trained on a relevant dataset such as ImageNet-1K. This method demonstrates superior performance on a unique benchmark dataset derived from Google Earth imagery, outperforming alternative techniques like anomaly detection methods, feature counting, and semi-supervised learning approaches. Notably, the proposed method achieves a high accuracy of 94.4% in identifying equipment on aerial images. 

  To evaluate the robustness of this method, the researchers conducted multiple experiments, including providing the model with artificially distorted images, manipulating the camera angles in the training data, and testing it on different equipment types. These experiments aimed to simulate real-world scenarios and assess the model's generalizability. 

  Building upon this work, the researchers explored several simplified approaches to facilitate the deployment of this technology. These included replacing the SwAV encoder with a pre-trained ResNet, reducing the computational requirements of the method, and developing a one-shot learning technique. 

  The researchers further extended the method to detect multiple types of equipment, applying a novel technique to improve the model's performance. 

  Finally, the researchers conducted a comprehensive comparison of their method with state-of-the-art techniques on a separate benchmark dataset of military equipment, demonstrating the method's versatility and generalizability.

  learning of representations by dynamically sampling negative examples from
  permutations of the training dataset. However, these permutations come with
  inherent biases, favoring transpositions over other permutations which in
  turn harms the learned representations. To address this issue, a new family
  of contrastive losses, called family $\mathcal{F}$, is proposed that can be
  applied without relying on biased dataset permutations. Furthermore, a
  specific loss function from family $\mathcal{F}$, called PCL, is developed
  that uses precomputed commutative permutations to free the method from
  expensive permutation sampling during training. When evaluated against
  current self-supervised learning techniques on various vision benchmarks, PCL
  represents a simple yet powerful approach that often surpasses the state-of-
  the-art results while requiring minimal hyperparameter adjustments. The
  empirical evidence suggests that PCL's success can be attributed to its
  capacity to capture structured geometric relationships within datasets.  The
  code for PCL is publicly available at https://github.com/keunhong/pcl.

However, the process of generating proposals in these methods is highly dependent on the pre-designed objectness confidence threshold, resulting in an imbalance of easy and hard proposals for the classification stage. This has been identified as a major drawback of these methods. In this study, a novel proposal generation mechanism called multi-scale feature clustering is proposed to address this issue. By incorporating three different feature types: low, middle and high level, the method is able to automatically eliminate background proposals and provide the classification stage with a more balanced set of proposals. In addition, the method has the capability to handle multiple scales of objects. In our experiments, the performance of our method was evaluated on the PASCAL VOC 2009 benchmark using a pre-trained VGG16 model, and the results showed that the method was able to achieve an mAP of 73.5% without any fine-tuning. When paired with the transfer learning technique, the method was able to achieve an mAP of 75.5%. In comparison to the state-of-the-art methods, the results showed that our method was able to provide a more consistent flow of proposals for the classification stage, resulting in an overall improvement in performance. Building upon a previous measurement by the ZEUS collaboration in 1996, who measured cross-sections at a centre-of-mass energy per nucleon of 18.6 GeV, a new analysis by the PHENIX collaboration increased the accessible range by two orders of magnitude, measuring at energies of 110 to 409 GeV per nucleon. We present here a detailed analysis of the rotation-related phenomena observed in the late-type active stars, based on data collected using the INTEGRAL satellite in the 5-70 keV energy range. Although extensive research has been done on elastic and permeable fractures, there is a lack of similar studies on brittle fractures.  In this research, we developed a comprehensive model for brittle fractures by combining high-resolution numerical simulations and data-driven machine learning techniques.  Specifically, we applied a combination of the level-set method and a deep learning framework to model the fracture propagation and surface geometry.  To account for the influence of Magma pressure, we introduced a new term into the governing equations, which effectively merged three distinct fluid flow regimes - Darcy flow, Darcy-Brinkman-Forchheimer-Stokes flow, and Driessen's lubrication theory.  Through numerical simulations, we demonstrated the validity and accuracy of our model in predicting fracture propagation and Magma flow through the crust.  In particular, we found that Magma pressure can significantly increase the surface area of fractures and facilitate higher rates of fluid transport.  In addition, we found that at very low Magma pressures, the flow regime transitions from Darcy flow to Driessen's lubrication theory, which is characterized by thin lubrication films surrounding the fracture surface.  Overall, our model provides a valuable tool for understanding the complex interactions between Magma pressure, fractures, and fluid flow in the Earth's crust.  In particular, it has the potential to greatly improve our ability to locate and extract Magma and hydrothermal resources.  In the future, we plan to extend our model to account for additional factors such as variable viscosities, heat transfer, and electrostatic interactions.  Furthermore, we aim to apply our model to real-world case studies, which will be crucial for optimizing resource extraction operations. Under this arrangement, each observation is defined by a multi-dimensional vector, yielding a tailored version of Spearman's test known as the block-Spearman test. The study provides a precise mathematical representation of the block-Spearman test's asymptotic distribution and offers a computationally efficient method for statistical analysis by approximating the test statistic's distribution using a deconvolution approach based on kernel estimation. 

  A novel aspect of the study involves the integration of a total variation minimization approach within the deconvolution process, aiming to enhance the accuracy of the test statistic's probability mass function recovery. The proposed method is validated through a comprehensive evaluation of its performance in simulated data experiments and is subsequently applied to analyze genomic data from Arabidopsis thaliana. The analysis utilizes the block-Spearman test to identify significant variations in the genome by considering the positions of methylated cytosine phthaloes relative to the nearby nucleotides. The study demonstrates that the improved method can effectively capture more precise empirical distribution functions for the test statistics in comparison to the standard approach. Furthermore, the total variation minimization approach is found to enhance the accuracy of the empirical distribution functions and facilitate the identification of significant features in the data. The application of the block-Spearman test to genomic data from Arabidopsis thaliana reveals key insights into the relationship between the location of methylation and the underlying cellular behavior. The study shows that the precise positioning of methylation plays a crucial role in gene expression and chromatin structure management. The results indicate that the block-Spearman test can effectively detect and analyze complex patterns within genomic data while providing a clear biological interpretation of the findings. Ultimately, the study highlights the potential of the block-Spearman test to be used as a powerful tool in analyzing diverse types of high-dimensional data across various scientific disciplines.

Variations in daily microgrid energy usage present an obstacle to achieving this goal, primarily due to higher energy demands in the morning and evening and lower or no consumption at night.  To address this, researchers have suggested integrating thermal energy storage systems (TESS) to capture energy during periods of low demand and release it during peak hours.  This paper examines the effectiveness of TESS in optimizing microgrids by aligning energy production with varying demand levels, with a specific focus on reducing natural gas consumption and costs.  To achieve this, a novel dynamic programming algorithm is presented, taking into account both short-term and long-term grid dynamics.  The proposed method is validated through simulations of a 10-kW microgrid linked to an electric vehicle charging station located in Toronto, Canada.  Simulation outcomes indicate that the optimal deployment of TESS can significantly mitigate the fluctuating nature of microgrid energy usage, ultimately leading to lower natural gas consumption and associated costs.  Notably, the optimal TESS capacity was found to be approximately 60 kilowatt-hours, allowing the microgrid to lower peak electricity costs by about 0.47 Canadian dollars per hour and ultimately reduce natural gas costs by around 0.24 Canadian dollars per hour.  This novel algorithm is expected to contribute positively to the efficient management and operation of microgrids. Research has shown that many real-world networks exhibit characteristics of a directed nature, with the pattern of connections (topology) playing a crucial role in determining the behavior of spreading processes. In this study, we analyze the diversity of directed network topologies that enable a limited number of independent spreading processes. Our research indicates that there are limited variations in topology types that facilitate multiple independent spreading processes and that this diversity declines as the number of independent spreading processes increases. Furthermore, we identify a theoretical model for determining the maximum capacity of directed network topologies that can accommodate multiple independent spreading processes. Additionally, we introduce a method to generate directed network topologies that maximize this capacity and demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through numerical simulations. Finally, we apply this model to undirected networks, showing that there are significantly more variations in topology types that enable multiple independent spreading processes when compared to directed networks. The outcomes of this research have implications for implementing immunization strategies in network systems. Specifically, we found that there are optimal numbers of nodes that can be vaccinated to maximize the capacity of directed network topologies that can accommodate multiple independent spreading processes. This finding is consistent across various types of spreading processes and network models. The techniques developed in this research can be applied to analyze the diversity of network topologies that enable multiple independent spreading processes in models beyond the compartmental model. For instance, we successfully utilized these methods to investigate the diversity of network topologies that enable multiple independent spreading processes in models of population movement and temporal networks. Ultimately, the results of this research contribute to a deeper understanding of the diversity of network topologies that enable multiple independent spreading processes, facilitating the development of more effective immunization strategies. The techniques and methodologies presented in this research can be applied to various types of networks, including food webs, transportation networks, and social media platforms, among others. Furthermore, the methods and models shown here can be extended to analyze the diversity of network topologies that enable multiple simultaneous spreading processes, such as epidemic outbreaks and biological invasions. In particular, we found that there are limited variations in topology types that enable multiple simultaneous spreading processes and that this diversity declines as the number of simultaneous spreading processes increases. This pattern, referred to as a "topological shape," has not been seen before in any other material and is predicted to play a crucial role in superconducting processes within these materials. Notably, it has been found that the topological shape is more visible near the point where electrons gain or lose energy than at other points, which could be attributed to the presence of flat regions in the energy curve. This phenomenon is more pronounced in cuprates and could be attributed to the strong interaction between electrons and the arrangement of atoms. This suggests that the topological shape is a key feature of materials exhibiting high-temperature superconductivity.
